questions.q: Identify the four supporting characters in "Mother's Day" and state one defining trait for each as established in the opening stage directions and early dialogue.
questions.a: The four supporting characters are: George Pearson (husband) — described as "solemn, self-important, pompous, heavy, slow-moving"; Doris Pearson (daughter) — "pretty girl in her early twenties... would be pleasant enough if she had not been spoilt"; Cyril Pearson (son) — "masculine counterpart of Doris," brisk and demanding; Mrs Fitzgerald (neighbour) — "older, heavier, strong and sinister personality," deep voice, Irish accent, smokes, knows fortune-telling. A wrong answer that describes them only by name or confuses their traits (e.g., calling Doris the "strong" one) reveals the student has not closely read the stage directions and character descriptions, which are essential evidence for character analysis at this level.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the body-swap device functions dramatically to reveal the true nature of the supporting characters' attitudes toward Mrs Pearson.
questions.a: The body-swap places Mrs Fitzgerald's assertive personality inside Mrs Pearson's body, stripping away the social expectation that "Mrs Pearson" must be subservient. When "Mrs Pearson" (actually Mrs Fitzgerald) refuses tea, smokes, insults Charlie Spence, and demands respect, the supporting characters' reactions — Doris's tears, Cyril's outrage, George's humiliation — expose their entitlement: they only respect authority, not the person. A wrong answer that treats the body-swap as merely a "funny plot twist" or "magic trick" misses its satirical purpose: it is a Brechtian alienation device that forces the audience to see the family's behaviour as learned and changeable, not natural.

questions.q: Using the PEEL structure (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link), write a short analytical paragraph showing how George Pearson's dialogue in the club scene (pp. 25-26) reveals his character and the play's critique of masculinity.
questions.a: Point: George Pearson embodies performative masculinity that masks insecurity. Evidence: He boasts of a "special snooker match night at the club" and "supper going," yet is devastated to learn they call him "Pompy-ompy Pearson" behind his back. Explanation: His pomposity ("I'm all for a steady going on") is a defence against ridicule; he prefers the club's false camaraderie to his wife's genuine presence. Link: This supports the play's theme that patriarchal authority is fragile and maintained by the silent labour of women like Mrs Pearson. A wrong answer that merely summarises the scene ("George goes to the club and gets upset") fails to analyse character function and thematic connection, which is the core skill at Class 11 level.

questions.q: Compare and contrast Doris and Cyril as "spoilt" children. How does the playwright differentiate their entitlement through specific behavioural details?
questions.a: Doris's entitlement is domestic and appearance-focused: she demands her "yellow silk" be ironed, cries when criticised, and defines herself by her boyfriend Charlie Spence. Cyril's entitlement is leisure- and labour-focused: he expects tea ready, his clothes mended, and spends money on "greyhound races and dirt tracks and ice shows." Both use the "eight-hour day" argument to justify being waited on, but Doris weaponises tears while Cyril weaponises sulking. A wrong answer that says "they are both selfish" without textual differentiation shows inability to perform close comparative analysis — a key board exam skill.

questions.q: Evaluate the dramatic necessity of Mrs Fitzgerald. Could the play achieve its resolution without her? Justify your answer with reference to structure and theme.
questions.a: Mrs Fitzgerald is dramatically indispensable. Structurally, she provides the inciting incident (fortune-telling), the mechanism (body-swap), and the resolution (enforcing the "firm hand" warning). Thematically, she represents the external perspective that the family cannot generate internally — she voices the feminist critique ("Husbands, sons, daughters should be taking notice of wives an' mothers") that Mrs Pearson cannot articulate. Without her, the play would lack both the catalytic event and the ideological anchor. A wrong answer that calls her "just a plot device" or "unnecessary because Mrs Pearson could have stood up for herself" ignores the play's central argument: systemic oppression requires external disruption; the victim cannot single-handedly dismantle the structure.

questions.q: Create a new scene (5-6 lines of dialogue) set one week after the play ends, showing how one supporting character has — or has not — changed. Use stage directions and character voices consistent with the text.
questions.a:
[Scene: Kitchen. Evening. George enters, hangs coat, pauses.]
George: [quietly] Annie? Tea?
Mrs Pearson: [not looking up from book] Kettle's on the stove, George. Mug's by the sink.
George: [hesitates, then moves to stove] Right. [Fills mug, carries it to table, sits opposite her] They're still laughing at the club. About "Pompy-ompy."
Mrs Pearson: [turns page] Are they?
George: [small smile] You were right. I'm not going tomorrow.
[Mrs Pearson looks up, nods once. Returns to book.]
A strong answer maintains character voices (George's slow speech, Mrs Pearson's new firmness), shows not tells the change, and uses the "Pompy-ompy" callback. A weak answer writes generic dialogue ("George: I've changed. Mrs Pearson: Good.") revealing inability to internalise characterisation techniques.
